blocks.content: You send a payment message through a queue. The consumer charges the card. Then something goes wrong on the network. Was the card charged once, not at all, or twice? The answer depends entirely on the delivery semantics of your messaging system.

Delivery semantics describe the guarantee a system gives about how many times a message is delivered when failures happen. There are three: at most once, at least once, and exactly once. Choosing the right one, and understanding what it really promises, is one of the most important decisions in a distributed system.

This matters because networks fail. Messages get lost, acknowledgements go missing, and consumers crash at the worst moment. Delivery semantics are precisely the rules for what happens in those messy situations.

You meet delivery semantics everywhere, even if the name is new. TCP retransmitting a lost packet, a payment API asking for an idempotency key, a queue redelivering a message, are all delivery semantics in action.
Getting this right is often the difference between a system that quietly double charges customers and one that does not, which is why it comes up in almost every serious design discussion.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028797-369338603.png
blocks.alt: The three delivery semantics, from lossy but simple to reliable but hard

blocks.content: 1. What Delivery Semantics Are
Delivery semantics are the promise a messaging system makes about how many times each message will be delivered to a consumer, especially when something fails along the way.

In a perfect world with no failures, every message would be delivered exactly once and there would be nothing to discuss. But real systems have network drops, timeouts, and crashes, and the semantics define how the system behaves in the face of those.
There are three levels, and they form a spectrum from weakest to strongest guarantee.

["At most once: a message is delivered zero or one times, so it may be lost but never duplicated","At least once: a message is delivered one or more times, so it is never lost but may be duplicated","Exactly once: a message affects the system once and only once, never lost and never duplicated"]
items: At most once: a message is delivered zero or one times, so it may be lost but never duplicated
At least once: a message is delivered one or more times, so it is never lost but may be duplicated
Exactly once: a message affects the system once and only once, never lost and never duplicated

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: Delivery semantics answer one question: when a failure happens, can a message be lost, duplicated, or neither? At most once may lose it, at least once may duplicate it, and exactly once does neither.
It helps to say the guarantees as counts. At most once means zero or one deliveries. At least once means one or more. Exactly once means precisely one effect.
Notice that at most once and at least once are opposites in what they risk. One risks losing a message, the other risks repeating it, and exactly once is the attempt to have neither.
2. The Root Cause: Networks and Failures
blocks.text: 2. The Root Cause: Networks and Failures

blocks.content: To understand the three semantics, you have to understand why exactly once is hard in the first place. It comes down to a simple, unavoidable problem: you can never be completely sure a message was received.

When a sender delivers a message and waits for an acknowledgement, two failures look identical. The message might have been lost before it arrived, or it might have arrived and been processed but the acknowledgement was lost on the way back. The sender sees the same thing in both cases: no acknowledgement.

Now the sender must choose. If it resends, it risks a duplicate, in case the message actually did arrive. If it does not resend, it risks a loss, in case the message really was lost. That single choice is the origin of the three semantics.

["Resend on no acknowledgement, and you get at least once, with possible duplicates","Do not resend, and you get at most once, with possible loss","There is no way to always be right, because the two failures are indistinguishable"]
items: Resend on no acknowledgement, and you get at least once, with possible duplicates
Do not resend, and you get at most once, with possible loss
There is no way to always be right, because the two failures are indistinguishable

blocks.title: The fundamental tradeoff
blocks.content: Because a lost message and a lost acknowledgement look identical to the sender, you must choose to risk either a duplicate or a loss. That impossibility is why delivery semantics exist at all.

Computer science has a name for this: the Two Generals Problem. Two parties communicating over an unreliable channel can never be completely certain the other received their last message, no matter how many acknowledgements they exchange.
That is not a limitation of a particular technology, it is a proven impossibility. So every real system picks a practical tradeoff rather than a perfect answer.
It is a strangely freeing idea once you accept it. You stop looking for a perfect delivery guarantee and start designing so that imperfect delivery is safe.
This is why an honest engineer treats exactly once with suspicion, and asks what a system really means when it claims that guarantee.
3. At Most Once
At most once is the weakest guarantee. The sender delivers a message and does not track it. If it is lost, it is simply gone, because there are no retries.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279066119-444608492.png
blocks.alt: At most once: no retry, so a crash before processing loses the message

blocks.content: This is the simplest and fastest approach. There is no acknowledgement to wait for, no state to track, and no risk of duplicates. The cost is that messages can silently disappear.
["Fast and simple, with no acknowledgements or retries","Never produces duplicates","Can lose messages when a failure happens","Acceptable only when losing a message occasionally does not matter"]
items: Fast and simple, with no acknowledgements or retries
Never produces duplicates
Can lose messages when a failure happens
Acceptable only when losing a message occasionally does not matter

blocks.content: It is the right choice for high volume, low value data where the occasional loss is harmless. A stream of live metrics or sensor readings is a good example: if one reading is dropped, the next one arrives a moment later and nobody cares.

blocks.title: When loss is fine
blocks.content: At most once suits things like live telemetry, where freshness matters more than completeness. It is never the choice for money, orders, or anything that must not vanish.

You can think of at most once as fire and forget. The classic example is UDP, which sends packets without tracking them, and application logging or metrics, where a dropped line is not worth the cost of guaranteeing delivery.
The appeal is pure speed and simplicity. With nothing to acknowledge, track, or retry, there is no overhead and no possibility of a duplicate.
The danger is silent loss. Nothing errors, the message just never arrives, which is why at most once is only safe when a missing message truly does not matter.
A quick gut check: if you would not mind this message vanishing without a trace, at most once is fine. If you would, it is not.
4. At Least Once

At least once is the practical default for most systems that care about their data. The sender keeps retrying until it receives an acknowledgement, so a message is never lost. The price is that it may be delivered more than once.
This happens whenever an acknowledgement is delayed or lost. The consumer processed the message fine, but the sender never heard back, so it sends again, and the consumer sees the same message twice.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279067760-324736306.png
blocks.alt: At least once: a lost acknowledgement causes a redelivery, so duplicates happen

blocks.content: ["Never loses a message, because it retries until acknowledged","Can deliver the same message more than once","The common default in queues, Kafka, and most brokers","Requires consumers to handle duplicates safely"]
items: Never loses a message, because it retries until acknowledged
Can deliver the same message more than once
The common default in queues, Kafka, and most brokers
Requires consumers to handle duplicates safely

blocks.content: Because duplicates are guaranteed to happen eventually at scale, at least once forces a discipline on you: your consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Get that right and duplicates stop mattering.

blocks.title: At least once needs idempotency
blocks.content: If you choose at least once, and you usually should, you are signing up to make your consumers idempotent. That single habit is what turns unavoidable duplicates into a non issue.
At least once is essentially how TCP behaves under the hood: keep resending until you get an acknowledgement. That reliability is exactly why it is the default for anything important.
It is the same instinct as certified mail. You would rather a letter arrive twice than not at all, and you deal with the rare double by recognising it.
The mental cost you accept in exchange is that duplicates are now your problem to handle, not the broker. You trade the risk of loss for the certainty of occasional repeats.
For almost every business system, that is the right trade, because losing an order or a payment is far worse than processing a duplicate you can detect and ignore.
This is why at least once is the workhorse of real systems. It gives a strong promise, never lose the message, and pushes the one remaining problem, duplicates, into a place you can solve cleanly.
5. Exactly Once: Myth and Reality
Exactly once is the dream: every message affects the system once and only once, no loss and no duplicates. It is also the most misunderstood guarantee in all of distributed systems.

The uncomfortable truth is that exactly once delivery is effectively impossible. Because of the network problem above, a sender can never know for certain whether to resend, so at the level of raw delivery you always face either loss or duplication.

What is actually achievable is exactly once processing. The message may be delivered more than once, but its effect on the system happens exactly once. The trick is to combine at least once delivery with deduplication or idempotency, so repeated deliveries are recognised and ignored.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028797-915375536.png
blocks.alt: Exactly once processing is really at least once delivery plus deduplication

blocks.content: ["Exactly once delivery, meaning physically delivered a single time, is effectively impossible","Exactly once processing, meaning the effect happens once, is achievable","It is built from at least once delivery plus idempotency or deduplication","When a system advertises exactly once, this is almost always what it means"]
items: Exactly once delivery, meaning physically delivered a single time, is effectively impossible
Exactly once processing, meaning the effect happens once, is achievable
It is built from at least once delivery plus idempotency or deduplication
When a system advertises exactly once, this is almost always what it means

blocks.title: The key distinction
blocks.content: Delivery and processing are different. You cannot guarantee a message is delivered exactly once, but you can guarantee it is processed exactly once, by deduplicating at least once delivery.

So when a vendor markets exactly once, the useful question is, exactly once of what, and within what boundary. Usually the honest answer is exactly once processing inside their own system, achieved with idempotency and transactions.

Understanding this saves you from a dangerous assumption. If you believe delivery is magically exactly once, you skip idempotency, and a single lost acknowledgement quietly doubles an effect in production.
Read every exactly once claim as exactly once processing within a boundary, and check what happens the moment your processing touches something outside that boundary.
6. Why Duplicates Happen
It is worth being crystal clear about where duplicates come from, because it explains the whole design of reliable systems.

The culprit is almost always the lost acknowledgement. The consumer receives the message, does the work, and sends an acknowledgement, but that acknowledgement is lost on the network. The broker, having heard nothing, assumes the delivery failed and sends the message again.

Notice that the work was already done. The duplicate is not because the message failed, it is because the confirmation failed. This is why you cannot simply avoid duplicates by being careful, they are a structural consequence of unreliable networks.

["A lost acknowledgement makes the broker redeliver a message that was already processed","A consumer timeout can trigger a redelivery while the first attempt is still running","A consumer crash after doing the work but before acknowledging causes a redelivery on restart","In every case, the fix is the same: recognise the repeat and make it harmless"]
items: A lost acknowledgement makes the broker redeliver a message that was already processed
A consumer timeout can trigger a redelivery while the first attempt is still running
A consumer crash after doing the work but before acknowledging causes a redelivery on restart
In every case, the fix is the same: recognise the repeat and make it harmless

blocks.content: Because these situations are unavoidable, the correct mindset is to expect duplicates and design for them, rather than hoping they will not occur. At small scale you might get lucky, but at large scale, duplicates are a certainty.
A useful way to internalise this is the phrase, hope is not a strategy. You will not avoid duplicates by writing careful code, because the cause is the network, not your logic.
So the professional stance is to assume the retry will happen, and to make sure that when it does, nothing bad results.
7. Idempotency: The Practical Path
Idempotency is the single most important tool for correctness in messaging, because it is what makes exactly once processing possible on top of at least once delivery.

An operation is idempotent if doing it multiple times has the same effect as doing it once. Setting a users email to a value is idempotent, because setting it twice leaves the same result. Adding ten dollars to a balance is not, because doing it twice adds twenty.

The general technique is to attach a unique id to every message and have the consumer remember which ids it has already processed. If a message arrives whose id has been seen, the consumer skips the work and simply acknowledges.

The subtle part is doing the work and recording the id atomically. If you process the message but crash before recording its id, a redelivery will process it again. Systems solve this by recording the id in the same transaction as the effect, so both happen together or not at all.

blocks.title: Idempotency beats chasing exactly once
blocks.content: Rather than fighting for perfect exactly once delivery, make your operations idempotent. It is simpler, more robust, and reaches the same outcome: the effect happens once no matter how many times the message arrives.

The atomicity of the effect and the id is the crux. If you charge the card and then crash before recording the id, a redelivery charges again. Recording the id in the same database transaction as the effect closes that gap.
This is exactly where the outbox pattern and transactional processing shine, because they let the side effect and the record of having done it commit together.
When the effect lives in an external system that cannot share your transaction, an idempotency key sent to that system does the same job, letting it recognise and ignore the repeat.

This is why so many payment and API providers expose an idempotency key. It hands you the exactly once processing guarantee as a simple feature: send the same key, and the operation runs at most one real time.
8. Deduplication Strategies
Idempotency and deduplication are two sides of the same coin. Deduplication is the mechanism for detecting a repeat, and there are a few common ways to do it.

["Unique id tracking: store processed message ids and skip any you have seen, the most general approach","Natural idempotency: design the operation so a repeat has no extra effect, like an upsert or a set operation","Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with a request, and the server ignores repeats of that key","Sequence numbers: reject any message older than the last one processed for a given key"]
items: Unique id tracking: store processed message ids and skip any you have seen, the most general approach
Natural idempotency: design the operation so a repeat has no extra effect, like an upsert or a set operation
Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with a request, and the server ignores repeats of that key
Sequence numbers: reject any message older than the last one processed for a given key

blocks.content: The right strategy depends on the operation. If the work is naturally idempotent, like writing a specific value, you may need no extra tracking at all. If it is not, like charging a card, you need explicit id or key based deduplication.

Idempotency keys are especially common in APIs. Payment providers, for example, let you send an idempotency key with a charge request, so if you retry after a timeout, the provider recognises the key and does not charge twice. It is exactly once processing exposed as an API feature.

blocks.title: Dedup needs a memory
blocks.content: Every deduplication approach needs somewhere to remember what has been seen, whether processed ids or the current state. That store, and how long it retains ids, is a real part of the design.

The retention window is a genuine tradeoff. Keep processed ids for too short a time and a late duplicate slips through, keep them forever and the store grows without bound. You size the window to the maximum realistic redelivery delay.
Where possible, natural idempotency is the cheapest option, because it needs no extra store at all. An upsert that sets a row to a value, or a set operation, is inherently safe to repeat.
9. Exactly Once in Real Systems
Some systems do advertise exactly once, and it is worth knowing what they actually provide.

Kafka offers an exactly once mode using idempotent producers, which prevent duplicate writes from producer retries, and transactions, which let a consume, process, and produce cycle commit atomically. Within the Kafka boundary, this gives genuine exactly once processing.

The catch is that these guarantees usually hold only inside the system. The moment your processing reaches out to an external database or an external API, that external effect is outside the transaction, and you are back to needing idempotency to make it safe.

["Kafka exactly once uses idempotent producers and transactions, valid within Kafka","Cloud queues often provide deduplication windows, ignoring repeats of the same id for a period","These help, but they rarely extend to external side effects like a database write or an email","So most real systems still rely on idempotent consumers as the general solution"]
items: Kafka exactly once uses idempotent producers and transactions, valid within Kafka
Cloud queues often provide deduplication windows, ignoring repeats of the same id for a period
These help, but they rarely extend to external side effects like a database write or an email
So most real systems still rely on idempotent consumers as the general solution

blocks.title: Exactly once has boundaries
blocks.content: A system exactly once guarantee usually stops at its own edge. For anything that touches the outside world, idempotency is still the tool that keeps effects from doubling.

You might wonder why not just use distributed transactions across everything. Protocols like two phase commit do exist, but they are slow, they hold locks, and they fail badly when a participant goes down, so most modern systems avoid them.
Instead, systems favour at least once plus idempotency, and patterns like the outbox and the saga, which achieve consistency without the fragility of a global transaction.
The takeaway is that correctness in distributed systems is usually built from small, local, idempotent steps, not from one big transaction that spans everything.

You will see this pattern named in many places, from the saga pattern to eventual consistency, but underneath they all accept the same reality: perfect coordination is impossible, so make each step safe to retry.
That acceptance is what lets large distributed systems stay correct without grinding to a halt on locks and coordination.
It is the quiet maturity of good distributed design: not chasing an impossible guarantee, but making failure ordinary and harmless.
So the industry has largely voted with its feet: idempotency, not distributed transactions, is the practical road to correctness.

If you do reach for coordination, patterns like the saga break a big operation into a series of local steps, each with a compensating action to undo it, rather than one global transaction. It is more work, but it survives failures gracefully.
10. Choosing the Right Semantic
With the three semantics understood, choosing between them comes down to two questions about your data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396029031-182471077.png
blocks.alt: A simple decision path for choosing a delivery semantic

blocks.content: ["Can you afford to lose a message? If yes, at most once is simplest and fastest","If not, you need at least once, so nothing is ever lost","Can you make processing idempotent or deduplicate? If yes, at least once plus idempotency gives you effectively exactly once","If you truly cannot tolerate any duplicate and cannot dedupe, you need a system with real exactly once support, accepting its cost"]
items: Can you afford to lose a message? If yes, at most once is simplest and fastest
If not, you need at least once, so nothing is ever lost
Can you make processing idempotent or deduplicate? If yes, at least once plus idempotency gives you effectively exactly once
If you truly cannot tolerate any duplicate and cannot dedupe, you need a system with real exactly once support, accepting its cost

blocks.content: In practice the answer for the vast majority of systems is the middle path: at least once delivery with idempotent consumers. It never loses data, it is widely supported, and idempotency neutralises the duplicates. Reserve at most once for disposable data and true exactly once for the rare cases that genuinely demand it.
The default that serves most systems well is at least once delivery plus idempotent processing. It loses nothing and, thanks to idempotency, behaves as if it were exactly once.

Consider a concrete case. For charging a card, you use at least once delivery with an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout never double charges. For emitting a live view count, at most once is fine, since a missed increment is invisible.
The same system often uses different semantics for different messages, matched to how much each one matters.
Choosing per message like this, rather than forcing one semantic on everything, is a sign of a mature design. You pay for reliability only where reliability is worth paying for.
11. Delivery vs Processing Semantics
A distinction runs through this whole topic that is worth stating on its own, because confusing the two is the source of most misunderstanding.
Delivery semantics are about how many times a message is handed to the consumer. Processing semantics are about how many times its effect is applied. They are not the same thing.

You can have at least once delivery but exactly once processing, and that combination is exactly what a well designed system aims for. The message may be handed over several times, but idempotency ensures the effect lands only once.

["Delivery: how many times the message reaches the consumer","Processing: how many times the effect actually happens","The realistic goal is at least once delivery with exactly once processing","When someone says exactly once, ask whether they mean delivery or processing"]
items: Delivery: how many times the message reaches the consumer
Processing: how many times the effect actually happens
The realistic goal is at least once delivery with exactly once processing
When someone says exactly once, ask whether they mean delivery or processing

blocks.title: This is the sentence that clears the confusion
blocks.content: You cannot control delivery counts perfectly, but you can control the effect. At least once delivery plus idempotency equals exactly once processing, and that is the real target.

This is why interviewers listen for the word processing. A candidate who says exactly once delivery is repeating a marketing phrase, while one who says at least once delivery with exactly once processing understands what is actually happening.
12. Ordering and Its Relationship
Delivery semantics are often discussed alongside ordering, because both are guarantees about how messages behave, and both get harder in a distributed system.

Ordering asks whether messages arrive in the order they were sent, while delivery semantics ask how many times they arrive. They are independent questions, but they interact. Retries in at least once delivery, for example, can reorder messages, since a redelivered message may arrive after later ones.

["Ordering and delivery semantics are separate guarantees that often interact","At least once retries can disturb ordering, delivering an old message after newer ones","Systems usually guarantee order only within a partition or per key, not globally","Idempotency plus per key ordering together give both correctness and sensible sequencing"]
items: Ordering and delivery semantics are separate guarantees that often interact
At least once retries can disturb ordering, delivering an old message after newer ones
Systems usually guarantee order only within a partition or per key, not globally
Idempotency plus per key ordering together give both correctness and sensible sequencing

blocks.content: The combined lesson from this whole area of messaging is consistent: assume at least once delivery, make consumers idempotent, and rely on per key ordering. Those three habits handle duplicates, losses, and reordering together.

It is worth noticing how the messaging chapters all converge on the same advice. Queues, pub sub, CDC, and delivery semantics all end at idempotent consumers and per key ordering, because those are the tools that make unreliable delivery safe.
If you remember one sentence from this page, make it this: assume at least once delivery and make your processing idempotent, and almost everything else falls into place.
Learn that pattern once and it applies to every messaging system you will ever touch.
That convergence is not a coincidence. It reflects the deep truth that in a distributed system you cannot prevent failures, you can only make your handling of them safe and repeatable.
13. Common Mistakes
Delivery semantics are subtle, and the mistakes around them are some of the most damaging in production.

["Assuming exactly once delivery is real and skipping idempotency, leading to double charges and duplicate effects","Choosing at most once for important data, then quietly losing messages","Acknowledging a message before the work is done, turning at least once into accidental loss","Making a non idempotent operation, like incrementing a balance, the consumer of an at least once queue","Not making the process and record the id step atomic, so a crash still causes reprocessing"]
items: Assuming exactly once delivery is real and skipping idempotency, leading to double charges and duplicate effects
Choosing at most once for important data, then quietly losing messages
Acknowledging a message before the work is done, turning at least once into accidental loss
Making a non idempotent operation, like incrementing a balance, the consumer of an at least once queue
Not making the process and record the id step atomic, so a crash still causes reprocessing

blocks.content: Almost every one of these traces back to a single misunderstanding: believing the system delivers each message exactly once. Once you accept that duplicates and losses are possible and design for them, these problems disappear.

blocks.title: The mindset that prevents the bugs
blocks.content: Treat every message as something that could arrive zero, one, or many times. Design so that loss is impossible where it matters, and duplicates are harmless everywhere. That mindset is what separates robust systems from fragile ones.

There is a common failure story worth remembering. A team assumes exactly once, ships a payment consumer with no idempotency, and everything works in testing where no acknowledgements are lost. In production, under load, one lost acknowledgement double charges a customer, and trust is damaged.

The fix is always the same and always cheap by comparison: an idempotency key and a check before acting. Building it in from the start costs almost nothing, while discovering the need in production is expensive.
14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 14. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: Delivery semantics are a favourite interview topic precisely because they reveal whether you understand distributed systems deeply or just superficially.
Name the three: I lay out at most once, at least once, and exactly once, and I explain that the choice is about whether loss or duplication is acceptable.
Debunk exactly once: I point out that exactly once delivery is effectively impossible, and what we really achieve is exactly once processing through idempotency.
Pick the default: For anything that matters I choose at least once delivery with idempotent consumers, which loses nothing and behaves as if exactly once.
Show the failure reasoning: I explain that a lost acknowledgement, not a lost message, is what causes duplicates, which demonstrates I understand why the guarantees exist at all.

Tie it to the outbox and idempotency: I connect delivery semantics to concrete tools, an idempotency key or the outbox pattern, which shows I can turn the theory into a design that will not double charge a customer.
